passage:
Monday. Parul made a meme of the school timetable with the caption 'Now with 12 periods of Sanskrit, so we can finally relax' and posted it in the class group. Fifteen people reacted with laughing faces.
Wednesday. Harish asked her at recess, slightly worried, "Is the Sanskrit thing real? My mother asked me." Parul stared at him. "It's a joke, Harish." He said, "It looked like a notice."
Saturday. Parul reposted the meme with a small line at the bottom: 'satire, not a real timetable'. Harish sent her a thumbs-up. She also took down a second meme she'd started that made fun of a boy's stammer. "That one's punching down," she told herself.

qa.q: How many people reacted to Parul's timetable meme?
qa.a: Fifteen people reacted with laughing faces.

qa.q: Why was Harish worried on Wednesday?
qa.a: He thought the meme might be a real notice, and his mother was asking him about it. He may also have felt embarrassed at being fooled.

qa.q: What did Parul do that made her memes safer?
qa.a: She added a label saying it was satire and removed the meme that mocked a boy's stammer.

qa.q: How might the boy with the stammer have felt if the second meme had been posted?
qa.a: He would probably have felt hurt and exposed, since it would have mocked something he cannot help.

grounding: Memes and satire convey shared attitudes economically, may be mistaken for fact, and can hurt if they mock vulnerable people.

passage: Keerthana, my mother used to say a joke has a direction, up or down. When I was young, our neighbourhood theatre group performed a street play where a tiny clerk mocked the corrupt officer, and the whole lane laughed until they wept. That was aimed up, at power. Then a group of boys drew a cartoon of the tea seller's limp and passed it around. That was aimed down, at someone who couldn't answer. I felt sick, though I laughed once, I'm ashamed to say. Today your memes are quicker, but the question stays the same: who is it laughing at, and can they take it? Also, put a note if it's satire, because not everyone knows. Ayesha.

qa.q: What did the tiny clerk do in the street play?
qa.a: The tiny clerk mocked the corrupt officer.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel about the cartoon of the tea seller?
qa.a: Ayesha felt sick, and ashamed of having laughed once, because the joke was aimed at someone who could not answer. It was mockery of a vulnerable person.

qa.q: What two questions does Ayesha suggest asking about a meme?
qa.a: Who the meme is laughing at, and whether that person can take it, plus adding a note when it is satire.

qa.q: How might the tea seller have felt about the cartoon?
qa.a: The tea seller may have felt hurt and embarrassed that people made fun of the limp.

grounding: An elder contrasts satire aimed at power with mockery of a vulnerable person, warning satire can be misread.

passage:
The school's new canteen menu had just doubled the price of samosas. Arohi had twenty minutes before the online class started and a burst of ideas.
She made a meme fast: a crying samosa in a crown, with the caption "Now available only to royalty. Apply with bank statement." She sent it to the class group. Laughs everywhere.
Fifteen minutes later Gopika messaged: "Uh, my mother's group is forwarding your meme. Some parents think the school actually wants bank statements."
Arohi's stomach dropped. The class was starting in five minutes.
She typed quickly in the class group: "This is a JOKE meme about samosa prices. The school has NOT asked for bank statements." She asked Gopika to forward that line to her mother's group, and messaged the canteen committee teacher too, just in case.
Then she logged in to class, heart still thumping.

qa.q: What did the meme's caption say?
qa.a: "Now available only to royalty. Apply with bank statement."

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when Gopika told her about the forwards?
qa.a: Arohi felt alarmed and anxious, her stomach dropping, because the satire had been taken as fact.

qa.q: What did Arohi do to fix the misunderstanding?
qa.a: She posted a clear note that it was a joke, asked Gopika to forward it to the parents' group, and told the canteen teacher.

qa.q: How might the parents in Gopika's mother's group have felt seeing the meme without context?
qa.a: They might have felt confused or worried that the school really wanted bank statements, since satire can look like fact out of context.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager's satirical meme conveying a shared complaint economically but being mistaken for fact.

passage:
Chandrika's friends in the Bengaluru apartment's study room were sharing clips on her phone. She found a parody video that was going around: a boy stammering through a school speech, with sped-up audio and a laugh track.
"This one's hilarious," Chandrika said, and sent it to the group.
Ishita didn't laugh. She put her pen down.
"My brother stammers," she said quietly. "People used to do that to him in the bus."
The room went still. Chandrika's face burned.
"I didn't think... I'm sorry."
"You didn't make it. But you shared it."
Chandrika opened the group and typed: "Deleting that clip. It mocks someone for stammering, not cool." She deleted it.
Later she sent Ishita one of her own memes instead, a cat labelled "me before board exams," and Ishita replied with a laughing face.

qa.q: What did the parody video show?
qa.a: A boy stammering through a school speech, with sped-up audio and a laugh track.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when Ishita mentioned her brother?
qa.a: Chandrika felt ashamed and embarrassed, her face burning, realising the clip mocked something that had hurt Ishita's family.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that repaired the moment?
qa.a: She apologised, deleted the clip, and told the group why it wasn't okay.

qa.q: What is it like for Ishita when a clip mocking stammering is shared as funny?
qa.a: It probably brings back the pain of watching her brother being mocked, making it hard to laugh along.

grounding: The scene shows a parody shared as humour hurting someone because it mocks a vulnerable person.

passage:
"Did you see my meme about the ward election?" Yash grinned. "Both candidates as cartoon roosters fighting over one pothole."
Irfan laughed. "Yeah, it's good. The pothole with a crown got me."
"Everyone's sharing it."
"Including my uncle."
"Nice!"
"Not nice. He sent it to the family group saying, 'See, even the kids know the candidates promised only one road.'"
Yash's grin slipped. "That's... not what I said. It's a joke."
"He thinks it's a fact."
"Should I delete it?"
Irfan thought. "Maybe just add a line. 'Satire, not news.' People can still laugh."
Yash typed it in and reposted. "It's weird. I made it to say what we all feel about the roads, not to spread something untrue."
"That's what's good about memes and what's scary," Irfan said.

qa.q: What did the meme show the candidates as?
qa.a: Both candidates as cartoon roosters fighting over one pothole.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Irfan told him about his uncle's message?
qa.a: Yash felt uneasy and a bit alarmed, his grin slipping, because his joke had been taken as a fact.

qa.q: What small step did Yash take to reduce confusion?
qa.a: He added a line saying "Satire, not news" and reposted it, so people could still laugh without mistaking it for fact.

qa.q: How might Irfan's uncle have seen the meme?
qa.a: He saw it as proof of something real about the candidates, not realising it was satire.

grounding: The dialogue shows a satirical meme sharing a common attitude economically but being mistaken for fact.

passage: Last term I became briefly famous for a meme. The canteen had raised samosa prices again, so I edited a picture of a school circular to say "Samosas now available on monthly instalment plan." I posted it in the class group and it spread through three batches by lunch. People loved it because it said what everyone felt without a speech. Then two things happened. A Class 7 parent phoned the office asking about the instalment plan; they'd thought it was real. And someone replied with their own version mocking Raju bhaiya, who runs the counter and walks with a limp. Aadhya messaged me: "Simran, yours was funny. That one isn't. He'll see it." My face went hot. I asked the group to delete the reply, and I added "SATIRE, not a real circular" to mine. Next day I bought two samosas at the new price and said sorry to Raju bhaiya anyway.

qa.q: What did Simran's meme say about samosas?
qa.a: It said samosas were now available on monthly instalment plan.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Aadhya's message arrived?
qa.a: Simran felt embarrassed and uneasy, face going hot, seeing the joke had led to something hurtful; there may also have been a sting that the satire was taken as fact.

qa.q: What did Simran do to limit the harm?
qa.a: Simran asked the group to delete the mocking reply, labelled the meme as satire, and apologised to Raju bhaiya in person.

qa.q: How might Raju bhaiya be affected by the reply meme?
qa.a: Being mocked for a limp in front of the students Raju bhaiya serves every day could feel humiliating, which is why Aadhya warned the meme would be seen.

grounding: It shows a teenager's satirical meme carrying a shared attitude, then being mistaken for fact and followed by a reply that mocks a vulnerable person.
